stem: Your team wants to standardize a custom `/generate-tests` command across all developers working on your React project. Where should you place the command file to ensure it's version controlled and available to all team members?

options.label: A
options.text: In ~/.claude/commands/ so each developer can customize it

options.label: B
options.text: In the project root as generate-tests.md

options.label: C
options.text: In .claude/commands/ within the project repository

options.label: D
options.text: In /usr/local/claude/commands/ for system-wide access

explanation: Project-scoped commands belong in .claude/commands/ within the repository. This ensures they're version controlled, shared across the team, and automatically available when working in that project. User-scoped commands (~/.claude/commands/) are for personal commands that shouldn't be shared.

stem: You're building a developer productivity agent that needs to handle 15 different legacy system documentation patterns, each requiring 200+ lines of specific instructions. The agent only uses 2-3 patterns per session. What's the most token-efficient approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Put all patterns in the main CLAUDE.md file for immediate availability

options.label: B
options.text: Create separate skills for each pattern with auto-invocation based on file extensions

options.label: C
options.text: Use a single skill with conditional logic to handle all patterns

options.label: D
options.text: Create individual skills for each pattern, invoked manually via slash commands

explanation: Skills are loaded on-demand, making them more token-efficient than CLAUDE.md for large, infrequently-used instructions. Individual skills allow precise loading of only needed patterns. Auto-invocation could trigger multiple skills unnecessarily, and a single conditional skill would still load all patterns.

stem: A colleague implements a `/code-review` skill that expects to access the current conversation history to understand previous code changes discussed. After deployment, the skill fails to reference earlier context. What's the fundamental issue?

options.label: B
options.text: The skill needs explicit context: fork configuration in frontmatter

options.label: C
options.text: Skills require allowed-tools: ['Read'] to access conversation history

options.label: D
options.text: The skill file is missing the version field in YAML frontmatter

options.label: A
options.text: Skills execute as isolated sub-agents without access to parent conversation context

explanation: Skills execute with fork context, meaning they run as isolated sub-agents without access to the parent conversation history. Any needed context must be explicitly provided in the skill invocation or instructions. The context: fork behavior is intentional for clean skill execution.

stem: You're creating a skill for generating API documentation. Which YAML frontmatter fields are required in your SKILL.md file?

options.label: A
options.text: name, description, allowed-tools

options.label: B
options.text: name, description, version

options.label: C
options.text: name, version, context

options.label: D
options.text: description, version, argument-hint

explanation: The required YAML frontmatter fields for a SKILL.md file are name, description, and version. The name becomes the slash command, description explains the skill's purpose, and version tracks changes. Fields like allowed-tools, context, and argument-hint are optional.

key_concept_tested: allowed-tools frontmatter for skill tool access
stem: Your `/refactor-component` skill needs to read existing files, write modified versions, and run tests to verify changes. Which frontmatter configuration enables these capabilities?

options.label: A
options.text: tools: ["Read", "Write", "Bash"]

options.label: B
options.text: permissions: ["file_read", "file_write", "shell_exec"]

options.label: C
options.text: allowed-tools: ["Read", "Write", "Bash"]

options.label: D
options.text: capabilities: ["Read", "Write", "Bash"]

explanation: The allowed-tools frontmatter field specifies which tools a skill can access. For file operations and test execution, you need Read, Write, and Bash tools. The field name is specifically 'allowed-tools', not 'tools', 'permissions', or 'capabilities'.

stem: A developer puts comprehensive coding standards (500+ lines) directly in CLAUDE.md, claiming "Claude needs this context for every interaction." The team reports slower response times. What's the core problem with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: CLAUDE.md should only contain project metadata, not detailed instructions

options.label: B
options.text: The standards should be split across multiple CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories

options.label: C
options.text: Large always-loaded context consumes tokens unnecessarily when standards aren't needed

options.label: D
options.text: Coding standards should be implemented as skills, loaded only when relevant

explanation: CLAUDE.md content is always loaded into context, consuming tokens even when not needed. Large instructional content like coding standards should be implemented as skills that load on-demand, improving token efficiency and response times. CLAUDE.md should contain frequently-needed, concise project information.

stem: You're creating a `/migrate-api` skill that requires users to specify the source version, target version, and migration strategy. How should you guide users on the expected input format?

options.label: A
options.text: Include detailed usage examples in the skill description

options.label: B
options.text: Add argument-hint: "source target strategy" to the frontmatter

options.label: C
options.text: Create separate skills for each migration path

options.label: D
options.text: Use input-validation: true in the frontmatter

explanation: The argument-hint frontmatter provides brief parameter guidance, but for complex inputs like API migration parameters, detailed usage examples in the description are more helpful. This gives users clear context on expected formats and options without cluttering the hint field.

stem: Your team uses a custom `/analyze-deps` command that needs to evolve with your project's dependency management practices. What's the primary benefit of placing this in .claude/commands/ versus ~/.claude/commands/?

options.label: A
options.text: Faster execution due to proximity to project files

options.label: B
options.text: Version control integration and team synchronization

options.label: C
options.text: Access to project-specific environment variables

options.label: D
options.text: Automatic activation when entering the project directory

explanation: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ are version controlled with the repository, ensuring all team members have the same command versions and can collaborate on improvements. User-scoped commands (~/.claude/commands/) are personal and not shared or versioned.

key_concept_tested: context fork isolation for skill execution
stem: You're designing a `/security-audit` skill that should analyze code without being influenced by previous conversation context about performance optimizations. Which execution model best serves this requirement?

options.label: A
options.text: Standard execution with full conversation context

options.label: B
options.text: Context: shared to maintain conversation awareness

options.label: C
options.text: Context: fork for isolated, unbiased analysis

options.label: D
options.text: Context: append to build on previous analysis

explanation: Context: fork creates an isolated sub-agent execution environment, perfect for security audits that should be unbiased by previous conversation context. This prevents performance optimization discussions from influencing security analysis, ensuring objective evaluation.

stem: A developer creates skills that auto-invoke based on file extensions: `/analyze-js` for .js files, `/analyze-ts` for .ts files, `/analyze-jsx` for .jsx files. Users report slow responses and irrelevant analysis when browsing code. What's the issue?

options.label: A
options.text: Auto-invocation triggers multiple skills simultaneously, causing context conflicts

options.label: B
options.text: Skills should use manual slash command invocation for precise control

options.label: C
options.text: File extension triggers are too broad, causing unnecessary skill activation

options.label: D
options.text: Auto-invocation loads skills even when users just want to browse, not analyze

explanation: Auto-invocation based on file extensions triggers skills whenever those files are accessed, even for simple browsing. This wastes tokens and provides unwanted analysis. Skills should be invoked intentionally when analysis is actually needed, not automatically on file access.

stem: You have a personal `/my-notes` command for quick note-taking that you don't want to share with your team. Where should this command be placed?

options.label: A
options.text: ~/.claude/commands/ for personal use only

options.label: B
options.text: .claude/commands/ but add it to .gitignore

options.label: C
options.text: .claude/personal/commands/ within the project

options.label: D
options.text: /tmp/claude/commands/ for temporary access

explanation: User-scoped commands belong in ~/.claude/commands/ and are personal to the individual user. They're not version controlled or shared with the team. Project-scoped commands (.claude/commands/) are meant for team collaboration and should be shared.

stem: Your team needs to organize 12 different code analysis skills (linting, security, performance, documentation, etc.). What's the most maintainable directory structure in .claude/skills/?

options.label: A
options.text: One SKILL.md file with all analysis patterns

options.label: B
options.text: Individual directories: lint-analyzer/SKILL.md, security-analyzer/SKILL.md, etc.

options.label: C
options.text: Categorized subdirectories: analysis/lint/SKILL.md, analysis/security/SKILL.md

options.label: D
options.text: Numbered files: 01-lint.md, 02-security.md in .claude/skills/

explanation: Each skill should have its own directory with a SKILL.md file (e.g., lint-analyzer/SKILL.md). This provides clear organization, makes skills easy to find and maintain, and follows the expected directory structure for skill discovery.

stem: A team puts all their development workflows (git conventions, testing patterns, deployment steps, code review checklist) totaling 800 lines in CLAUDE.md, saying "Claude needs to know our full process." What's the efficiency problem?

options.label: A
options.text: CLAUDE.md should be limited to 100 lines maximum

options.label: B
options.text: All content loads into every conversation, wasting tokens when specific workflows aren't needed

options.label: C
options.text: The content should be split into separate CLAUDE.md files per workflow

options.label: D
options.text: Workflow-specific content should be implemented as on-demand skills

explanation: CLAUDE.md content is always loaded, consuming tokens regardless of relevance. Large workflow documentation should be split into skills that load only when needed. This improves token efficiency and response times while maintaining access to detailed process information.

key_concept_tested: skill naming and slash command conventions
stem: You're creating skills for database operations: schema migration, data seeding, backup creation, and query optimization. What naming convention best supports team usability?

options.label: A
options.text: db-migrate, db-seed, db-backup, db-optimize for clear prefixing

options.label: B
options.text: migrate-schema, seed-data, create-backup, optimize-queries for action-first naming

options.label: C
options.text: database-migration, database-seeding, database-backup, database-optimization for full clarity

options.label: D
options.text: migrate, seed, backup, optimize with database context in skill descriptions

explanation: Concise, action-focused names (migrate, seed, backup, optimize) are easier to type and remember. The database context should be clear from the skill descriptions and directory organization. Overly verbose names create friction in daily usage.

key_concept_tested: skill version field purpose and usage
stem: Your `/test-generator` skill has evolved through several iterations with different testing frameworks and patterns. What's the primary purpose of the version field in the YAML frontmatter?

options.label: A
options.text: Enables Claude to automatically update skills to the latest version

options.label: B
options.text: Tracks changes and helps with debugging skill behavior over time

options.label: C
options.text: Determines skill execution priority when multiple versions exist

options.label: D
options.text: Controls compatibility with different Claude model versions

explanation: The version field in skill frontmatter is primarily for tracking changes and helping with maintenance and debugging. It provides a clear history of skill evolution and helps identify which version might have introduced issues or changes in behavior.

key_concept_tested: skill tool requirements and allowed-tools configuration
stem: Your `/deploy-staging` skill needs to read configuration files, execute deployment scripts, search for environment variables in multiple files, and create deployment logs. Which allowed-tools configuration is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: ["Read", "Write", "Bash", "Grep"]

options.label: B
options.text: ["Read", "Bash", "Grep", "Glob"]

options.label: C
options.text: ["Write", "Bash", "Grep", "Glob"]

options.label: D
options.text: ["Read", "Write", "Bash", "Grep", "Glob"]

explanation: The skill needs Read (config files), Write (deployment logs), Bash (deployment scripts), and Grep (searching for environment variables). Glob isn't necessary since the skill can use Read for specific files and Grep for searching within them.

stem: A developer creates a `/fix-bug` skill that references "the error we discussed earlier" and "the previous solution attempt" in its instructions. Users report the skill seems confused and asks for context that was already provided. What's the fundamental misunderstanding?

options.label: A
options.text: The skill needs context: shared instead of the default fork behavior

options.label: B
options.text: Skills execute in isolation and cannot access previous conversation context

options.label: C
options.text: The skill description should include all necessary context instead of referencing conversation history

options.label: D
options.text: Skills require explicit context passing through argument-hint parameters

explanation: Skills execute with fork context (isolation) by default and cannot access previous conversation context. The skill instructions should be self-contained and not reference earlier discussion. Any needed context must be explicitly provided in the skill invocation or built into the instructions.

key_concept_tested: balancing CLAUDE.md vs skills for project context
stem: Your legacy system integration project has: core API patterns (used in 90% of interactions), 8 specialized data transformation patterns (used occasionally), and emergency procedures (rarely needed). How should you organize this information?

options.label: A
options.text: Put everything in CLAUDE.md for comprehensive context

options.label: B
options.text: Core patterns in CLAUDE.md, transformations and procedures as separate skills

options.label: C
options.text: Create skills for all patterns to maximize token efficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Use a single comprehensive skill with all patterns and procedures

explanation: Frequently used core patterns (90% usage) belong in CLAUDE.md for immediate availability. Occasional-use transformations and rare emergency procedures should be skills to avoid token waste. This balances accessibility with efficiency.

key_concept_tested: slash command file naming and discovery
stem: You want to create a `/generate-docs` command for your project. What should be the filename and location for this command?

options.label: A
options.text: .claude/commands/generate-docs.md

options.label: B
options.text: .claude/commands/generate-docs/command.md

options.label: C
options.text: .claude/generate-docs.md

options.label: D
options.text: .claude/commands/generate-docs

explanation: Project-scoped slash commands are placed directly in .claude/commands/ directory with the command name as the filename (generate-docs.md). The filename becomes the slash command name (/generate-docs).

stem: You're creating a `/analyze-performance` skill for identifying bottlenecks in legacy codebases. The skill handles CPU profiling, memory analysis, and database query optimization. What makes for the most effective description?

options.label: A
options.text: "Analyzes code performance"

options.label: B
options.text: "Comprehensive performance analysis including CPU, memory, and database optimization for legacy systems"

options.label: C
options.text: "Performance analyzer - CPU/memory/DB"

options.label: D
options.text: "Identifies performance bottlenecks in code"

explanation: The description should be specific about capabilities (CPU, memory, database) and context (legacy systems) to help users understand when to use the skill. Generic descriptions don't provide enough information for effective skill selection.

stem: A developer creates separate skills for every minor code operation: `/add-import`, `/remove-import`, `/format-function`, `/add-comment`, `/remove-comment`. The team complains about too many slash commands to remember. What's the architectural issue?

options.label: A
options.text: Skills should be grouped by programming language instead of operation type

options.label: B
options.text: Over-granular skills create cognitive overhead without meaningful isolation benefits

options.label: C
options.text: These operations should be combined into broader skills like `/refactor-code` or `/clean-imports`

options.label: D
options.text: Individual operation skills should use auto-invocation instead of manual commands

explanation: Over-granular skills create unnecessary complexity and cognitive load. Related operations should be grouped into cohesive skills (e.g., import management, code formatting) that provide meaningful functionality while remaining discoverable and manageable.

stem: Your `/migrate-database` skill accepts multiple parameters: source database type, target database type, migration strategy (full/incremental), and optional table filters. What's the most helpful argument-hint format?

options.label: A
options.text: "source target strategy [tables]"

options.label: B
options.text: "<source_db> <target_db> <strategy> [table_filter]"

options.label: C
options.text: "database migration parameters"

options.label: D
options.text: "source_database target_database migration_strategy table_filters"

explanation: The argument-hint should use clear parameter names with angle brackets for required parameters and square brackets for optional ones. This format immediately shows users what's required vs optional and provides meaningful parameter names.

stem: You want to create a skill called "api-tester" for testing REST endpoints. What's the correct file structure?

options.label: A
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester.md

options.label: B
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester/skill.md

options.label: C
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester/SKILL.md

options.label: D
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester/API-TESTER.md

explanation: Skills must be organized in individual directories within .claude/skills/, with the skill definition in a file named SKILL.md (uppercase). The directory name becomes the skill name and slash command.

stem: You're building a `/setup-environment` skill that needs to: check if directories exist, create missing directories, copy template files, modify configuration files, and run initialization scripts. Which tools are essential?

options.label: A
options.text: Read, Write, Bash only

options.label: B
options.text: Read, Write, Bash, Glob

options.label: C
options.text: Write, Bash, Glob only

options.label: D
options.text: Read, Bash, Grep, Glob

explanation: The skill needs Read (check files/configs), Write (create/modify files), Bash (run scripts, create directories), and Glob (find template files). Grep isn't needed for this setup workflow, but Glob is essential for template file discovery.

stem: A team configures their `/security-scan` skill to auto-invoke whenever any .js file is opened, claiming "security should always be checked." Developers report constant unwanted security analysis during normal coding. What's the design flaw?

options.label: A
options.text: Auto-invocation should trigger on file save, not file open

options.label: B
options.text: Security scanning should be a manual process triggered intentionally

options.label: C
options.text: The trigger should be more specific to security-sensitive file patterns

options.label: D
options.text: Auto-invocation should only trigger for modified files, not opened files

explanation: Security scanning is a deliberate analysis activity that shouldn't auto-trigger during normal development workflow. Auto-invocation on file operations creates noise and interrupts the development process. Security scans should be intentionally invoked when needed.

key_concept_tested: personal vs team skill organization strategy
stem: Your team has shared code analysis skills, but you also have personal productivity shortcuts that wouldn't be useful to others. How should you organize these different types of skills?

options.label: A
options.text: All skills in project .claude/skills/ with personal ones marked as such

options.label: B
options.text: Team skills in project .claude/skills/, personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/

options.label: C
options.text: All skills in ~/.claude/skills/ for consistency

options.label: D
options.text: Team skills in project .claude/skills/, personal shortcuts as user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/

explanation: Team-relevant skills belong in the project's .claude/skills/ for version control and sharing. Personal productivity shortcuts are better as user-scoped commands (~/.claude/commands/) since they're simple, personal, and don't need the complexity of skill structure.

stem: You need to create a simple text transformation that converts camelCase to snake_case. This is a straightforward, stateless operation with no tool requirements. What's the most appropriate implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: A skill with detailed transformation logic in SKILL.md

options.label: B
options.text: A slash command with inline transformation instructions

options.label: C
options.text: Include the transformation pattern in CLAUDE.md

options.label: D
options.text: A user-scoped command for personal use

explanation: Simple slash commands are best for straightforward operations without complex logic or tool requirements. Skills are more appropriate for complex workflows that need structured instructions, tool access, or detailed processing steps.

stem: Your `/code-review` skill has grown from 50 lines to 300 lines as your team added more review criteria. Team members report it's becoming less focused and harder to maintain. What's the best refactoring approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Split into focused skills: `/review-security`, `/review-performance`, `/review-style`

options.label: B
options.text: Move detailed criteria to separate documentation and keep the skill concise

options.label: C
options.text: Create a master skill that delegates to specialized sub-skills

options.label: D
options.text: Convert to multiple slash commands for each review type

explanation: Large skills become unwieldy and less effective. The core skill should remain focused on the review process, with detailed criteria moved to referenced documentation. This maintains usability while preserving comprehensive guidance.

stem: A developer implements a `/continue-refactoring` skill with `context: shared` expecting it to automatically continue from previous refactoring discussions. The skill still asks for context about what needs refactoring. What's the misconception?

options.label: A
options.text: Context: shared doesn't exist; skills always use context: fork

options.label: B
options.text: Context: shared requires explicit conversation history passing

options.label: C
options.text: Skills need context: inherit to access previous conversation

options.label: D
options.text: The skill needs allowed-tools: ['Memory'] to access conversation history

explanation: Skills execute with context: fork (isolation) by design. There is no context: shared option. If continuation is needed, the skill must be designed to accept context as parameters or the conversation should continue without invoking an isolated skill.

key_concept_tested: optimizing skill loading and token usage
stem: Your development team has 20 different skills for various tasks. Developers report that Claude sometimes seems slower and uses more tokens than expected. What's the most likely cause and solution?

options.label: A
options.text: Too many skills are auto-invoking; switch to manual invocation only

options.label: B
options.text: Skills are too large; break them into smaller, focused skills

options.label: C
options.text: Some frequently-used skill content should be moved to CLAUDE.md

options.label: D
options.text: Skills should be consolidated into fewer, comprehensive skills

explanation: If certain skill content is used very frequently, it might be more efficient in CLAUDE.md to avoid repeated loading. The key is identifying which content is used often enough to justify always-loaded context versus on-demand skill loading.

key_concept_tested: slash command vs skill execution model differences
stem: What's the key execution difference between a slash command and a skill when invoked by a user?

options.label: A
options.text: Slash commands run in the main conversation context, skills run in isolated sub-agents

options.label: B
options.text: Slash commands are faster, skills provide more detailed responses

options.label: C
options.text: Slash commands can't access tools, skills can use allowed-tools

options.label: D
options.text: Slash commands are user-scoped only, skills are always project-scoped

explanation: The fundamental difference is execution context: slash commands execute within the ongoing conversation context, while skills execute as isolated sub-agents (context: fork) without access to previous conversation history.

key_concept_tested: skill error handling and robustness design
stem: Your `/deploy-to-staging` skill occasionally fails due to network timeouts or missing environment variables. Users want better error handling. What's the most robust approach within the skill design?

options.label: A
options.text: Add retry logic and validation checks directly in the skill instructions

options.label: B
options.text: Include error handling patterns and diagnostic steps in the skill workflow

options.label: C
options.text: Create separate skills for error recovery and diagnostics

options.label: D
options.text: Use allowed-tools: ['Error'] to enable automatic error handling

explanation: Skills should include error handling patterns and diagnostic steps in their workflow instructions. This guides Claude to check prerequisites, validate inputs, and provide helpful error diagnostics when issues occur, making the skill more robust and user-friendly.

stem: A developer puts detailed Git workflow instructions (branching strategy, commit message format, PR templates, merge procedures) totaling 400 lines in CLAUDE.md, reasoning "developers need this context for every code interaction." What's the architectural problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Git workflows should be in separate .gitconfig files, not CLAUDE.md

options.label: B
options.text: CLAUDE.md should only contain 50-100 lines of essential project context

options.label: C
options.text: Detailed workflows should be skills, with only essential patterns in CLAUDE.md

options.label: D
options.text: The content should be split across multiple CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories

explanation: CLAUDE.md should contain frequently-needed, concise project context. Detailed workflow instructions are better as skills (e.g., `/git-workflow`, `/create-pr`) that load only when needed, keeping the always-loaded context lean and relevant.

stem: Your team has created 15 useful skills, but adoption is low because developers don't know which skills exist or when to use them. What's the most effective solution for improving skill discoverability?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a `/list-skills` command that shows all available skills

options.label: B
options.text: Add a skills overview section to the main CLAUDE.md file

options.label: C
options.text: Set up auto-invocation for commonly needed skills

options.label: D
options.text: Create a master skill that can invoke other skills based on user requests

explanation: Adding a concise skills overview to CLAUDE.md ensures developers see available skills in every interaction without consuming excessive tokens. This provides constant visibility while keeping the information accessible and up-to-date with the project context.
